materials.text: Woodworking, household work and seafaring depended on material skill and knowledge of local conditions.

knowledge.text: Makah oral history and tribal interpretation belong alongside excavation; recovered material remained with the Tribe.

custody.text: Waterlogged material, disputed burial dates and a later archival photograph establish different facts.

interval.label: Reported house-burial estimates: c. 1560 or 1700; disputed
interval.note: Bounds describe differing published estimates for burial of houses, not the village’s occupation or a 140-year-long slide. SAH lists 1560/1700; WSU discusses 1700 as likely; the Makah museum reports 500±50 BP radiocarbon age, which is not silently converted to a calendar year.

alternatives.label: SAH reports 1560 or 1700 CE burial estimates; neither is village occupation.
Makah museum reports 500±50 BP radiocarbon age; WSU discusses likely 1700 correlation. These have different methods/scopes.

question: What survives when wooden things are buried—and who should interpret them?
summary: Mud preserved wooden household belongings at Ozette unusually well. Cedar working, food getting, storage and life in large houses can be investigated together. Makah oral history and the community’s custody of the recovered material are central to this account. The burial chronology is disputed, and later photographs of Makah life are labeled as later evidence.

sections.title: Preservation changes what history can see
sections.text: The Makah museum describes a storm exposing wooden artifacts in 1969–70 and a collaborative excavation beginning in April 1970. Normally perishable material survived in the mud. A rich wooden assemblage can correct a picture dominated by stone tools, but survival is still selective. What was preserved beneath part of the village is not a complete inventory of everything used by every Makah household.

citations.locator: Storm exposure, April 1970 excavation and waterlogged preservation

sections.title: A canoe joins craft and environmental knowledge
sections.text: The Tribe’s construction account describes hollowing cedar and steaming the sides rather than cutting away all their strength. Replaceable hardwood strips protected canoe sides found at Ozette. Navigation also relied on weather, swells and landmarks. Those are connected forms of expertise, not a choice between technology and knowledge. The account says sails were not found in the deposits; that absence does not securely date the invention or arrival of sails.

citations.locator: Makah Canoe Construction and Ensuring a Safe Journey

sections.title: Do not give the slide a false birthday
sections.text: Published accounts do not all give the same burial date. SAH presents 1560 or 1700; WSU discusses a likely relationship with the 1700 earthquake. The Makah museum reports a radiocarbon estimate in years BP. These claims require attention to samples, calibration and event correlation. The plotted range marks disagreement between reported calendar estimates. It is neither the village’s entire history nor an exact duration of a disaster.

sections.title: Belongings stayed in the community
sections.text: Makah oral history described a great slide before excavation. The museum explains that recovered material remained on the reservation and that the cultural center arose from the Tribe’s wish to curate and interpret it. This changes the question from who discovered a lost people to how different forms of evidence are studied together. The later Curtis photograph names Light House Joe; it does not depict the ancient burial event or identify a particular excavated canoe.

sections.title: A sequence of material decisions
sections.text: Read the Tribe’s construction account in three stages: shape cedar, use steam to flare the sides, then protect the edges that take wear. The account explains why retaining the grain matters and identifies replaceable hardwood gunwales on canoe sides found at Ozette. Making was not finished forever when a canoe first floated: parts could wear and be renewed. This sequence is publicly described knowledge, not a reconstruction of the boat in the later photograph.

claims.text: Makah oral history recalls a slide that buried part of Ozette. Researchers disagree about when it happened. The village has a longer history than the burial of these houses.

returnPrompt: Compare a wooden object preserved in mud with a later photograph. What different questions could each answer?

deeperReading.title: A material sequence is not a newly recovered scene
deeperReading.text: The Tribe’s public account explains how steam and wood grain connect: flaring softened sides avoids weakening them by cutting across the grain. It also names protective strips that could be replaced after paddling wear. These are reasons for choices and maintenance, rather than a picture of one recorded carver’s day. Only the gunwale statement is explicitly attached to Ozette finds in this passage. Neither the account nor the preserved later photograph supplies the dimensions, maker, work duration or full history of a particular excavated canoe.

deeperReading.title: Custody and permission are part of interpretation
deeperReading.text: The Makah museum presents the recovered collection through oral history and the Tribe’s desire to care for and interpret it. The museum connects the houses and household objects to a place Makah people remember and care for today. The setting and the age of the slide answer different questions. Researchers have proposed different calendar dates for the burial. A later photograph can show a canoe at the time the camera was used, while the excavated fittings carry evidence of earlier work.

evidenceReading.title: Shape, steam and replace: read a public material-work account
evidenceReading.introduction: These three editorial paraphrases form a material-work reading sequence. They use the Tribe’s public explanation, not a copied plan, new experiment or instruction to reproduce a cultural object.

items.label: Shape the cedar
items.text: The Tribe’s public account describes hollowing a red-cedar log. This stage removes material, but the desired final width was not obtained simply by carving away every part of the sides.
items.interpretation: Material removal is one part of making. The source’s account of construction should not be assigned automatically to every object or household.

items.label: Use heat to change the shape
items.text: Water and heated rocks supplied steam; the softened sides could be flared while retaining straight-grain strength. This explains a material decision in the account, not a measured procedure recovered from the later photograph.
items.interpretation: The reason for using heat concerns wood structure. No exact temperature, tool kit, timing or measured geometry is supplied here.

items.label: Protect a part that wears
items.text: The account identifies hardwood gunwales laced to canoe sides found at Ozette. These protective strips took wear from paddling and could be replaced. Maintenance belongs alongside initial making.
items.interpretation: This passage specifically connects a replaceable protective part with Ozette finds. It does not identify the later photograph’s boat as an excavated specimen.

familyActivity.title: A part that can be renewed
steps: Look at the later photograph. Describe the person, long pole and boat without calling it a view of the buried village. Keep its qualified place and later date attached.

Read this capsule from the Tribe’s public account: makers hollowed red cedar, then steamed the sides so they could flare while retaining the strength of the grain. Canoe sides found at Ozette had protective hardwood edge strips called gunwales. The strips took paddling wear and were easy to replace.

Make three text cards: “shape,” “change with heat” and “protect and replace.” Put the capsule’s statements in order. Explain why a replaceable strip could help maintain a canoe. Which parts of this sequence can the photograph alone prove?
familyActivity.explanation: The capsule supplies the sequence and the grain-strength explanation. Replacing a worn protective strip could renew that part without replacing the whole side. The photograph permits a description of a later boat and named person; it cannot show past heating, prove the construction sequence or identify an excavated Ozette canoe. The task uses public explanatory text without copying a design or carrying out a construction procedure.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author checking; not independent historian or Makah community approval
review.scope: The Tribe’s public account explains canoe construction and the care of the collection. The 4 November review pairs the museum’s description of the slide with the archaeological dating discussion on printed p. 84 of Gavin and colleagues’ report. The modern excavation has a separate chronology.
limitations: The c. 1560/1700 burial alternatives and 500±50 BP remain distinct reported claims; no new calendar conversion, assay inspection, calibration or earthquake correlation is performed. Village life and contemporary Makah knowledge are not reduced to a disaster date.

The SAH, WSU and Library of Congress pages returned 403 during this consultation and were not retried or bypassed. Their complete 27 October source records, access dates and qualifications remain unchanged. Only the museum and Tribe’s accessible public bodies receive selected renewals.

The later photograph was actually inspected but not freshly verified against an accessible LOC catalogue. Exact exposure place/date, boat identity and a connection to any excavated specimen remain qualified; all original rights/date fields and image bytes are retained.

The material-work sequence is a paraphrase of a public tribal account, not a copied plan, source geometry, experimental reconstruction or permission to reproduce restricted knowledge. No new image, annotation, route, numeric locator, museum reproduction or visit instruction is supplied. A stale closure banner is not current visiting advice.
